explanation:
## Two small functions, each with one job

```cpp
int min2(int a, int b)
{
    return a < b ? a : b;
}

int min3(int a, int b, int c)
{
    return min2(a, min2(b, c));
}
```

`min3` does not compare anything itself. It says "the smallest of three is the
smaller of the first and the smallest of the other two", which is the definition
written down. That is what building on a smaller piece buys you: the second
function is a sentence rather than a chain of comparisons.

## The conditional operator

```cpp
return a < b ? a : b;
```

reads as "if `a < b` then `a` else `b`". It is an **expression**, so it has a
value and can sit in a `return`. The `if` version is identical in meaning:

```cpp
if (a < b) return a;
else       return b;
```

Four lines instead of one. Use whichever reads better; for something this small
the conditional usually does, and for anything with a side effect the `if`
always does.

## Why `<` and not `<=`

For a minimum it makes no difference to the answer — if `a == b` either one is
the minimum — so either works here. It matters when the values carry something
besides their order. Sorting records by key with `<=` instead of `<` makes the
sort unstable, so equal keys can come out in a different order than they went
in. Habitually writing `<` costs nothing and avoids the question.

## The positions the tests check

| Input | Smallest is | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `1 2 3` | first | a chain that forgets to consider `a` fails here |
| `3 2 1` | last | and one that never reaches `c` fails here |
| `2 1 3` | middle | the one people miss |
| `7 7 3` | ties above the minimum | `<` against `<=` |
| `5 5 5` | all equal | nothing to distinguish |

Three positions times a tie case is why there are seven hidden tests for a
three-line function. A broken comparison chain usually gets one or two
positions right, which is exactly why testing only `4 9 2` tells you nothing.

## What the standard library already has

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
std::cout << std::min({ a, b, c }) << "\n";
```

`std::min` takes two arguments, or an initialiser list for any number. In real
code that is what you would write, and knowing the library is a large part of
being quick in C++.

Writing it yourself once is still worth it — the structure (a small function,
reused, built on a smaller one) is the thing being practised, not the
comparison.
